name: Lérins Press
tagline: The publishing arm of Mere Catholicity

motto.latin: Quod ubique, quod semper, quod ab omnibus creditum est.
motto.english: What has been believed everywhere, always, and by all.

about: Lérins is a small island off the coast of Cannes. Early in the fifth century Honoratus founded a monastery there, and it became a school for the Church in Gaul. Bishops came out of it, Hilary of Arles, Eucherius of Lyon, Lupus of Troyes and Caesarius of Arles among them, and so did books.
One of its monks, Vincent, wrote a short book there in 434 for telling the faith of the Church from the novelties pressed on it. Its test is the one this house is named for.

hope.heading: Vincent's test today
paragraphs: Lérins Press is an ecumenical publishing project, and an eclectic one. It is the publishing arm of merecatholicity.com, an app and a community of Christians who pray and work for the reunion of Christendom: the Roman Catholic Church, the Eastern Orthodox, the Assyrian and Oriental Orthodox churches, the Anglicans, the Lutherans, the Presbyterians and the rest. We put Vincent's test to the divided Church of our own day.

It still finds an answer. For the first thousand years, before East and West split in 1054 and long before the Reformation, Christians read the same Bible, said the same Nicene Creed and kept the same seven great councils, and every one of these churches holds them still. That is ground enough to stand on together. What any one church has added since can wait until the whole Church comes to agree on it. This is a conservative ecumenism: the moral consensus of the Fathers is kept entire, and no new church is founded.

That is why the shelves look as they do. Calvin stands beside Newman, the Westminster Confession beside John of Damascus, Luther beside Augustine, each church's classics in its own words. They are the best introduction one Christian can give another to what the others believe, and the first step toward talking as brothers again.

We sell high-quality paperbacks to support our mission. Each is a classic from the library at merecatholicity.com, newly typeset, with a new introduction and notes, made to last on the shelf. The library itself stays free to read online. Buying a Lérins Press book is the best way to support the work.

collections.name: Lérins Newman
collections.tagline: The works of John Henry Newman, Anglican and Catholic
about: John Henry Newman (1801 to 1890) lived forty-four years in the Church of England and forty-five in the Catholic Church, and wrote through both. At Oxford he led the movement that called the Church of England back to the Fathers. Reading them, he came to believe that their Church was the Church of Rome, and in 1845 he was received into it. He died a cardinal, and was canonized in 2019.

He argued with Vincent of Lérins all his life: how the faith held everywhere, always and by all can grow without becoming something else. Lérins Newman prints his works in three parts, the Anglican years, the Catholic years, and the essays, sketches and verse he gathered late in life, numbered in that order, so each book shows where it stands in one life.

collections.name: Lérins Creeds
collections.tagline: What each communion confesses, in its own words
about: What each communion actually confesses, in its own words: the ecumenical symbols, the Roman and Eastern standards, and the Protestant confessions, the originals beside their English.

Lérins Creeds prints them to be read side by side: Philip Schaff's Creeds of Christendom in its three volumes, the decrees of Trent, the Thirty-Nine Articles, the Book of Concord and the Westminster standards.

collections.name: Lérins Fathers
collections.tagline: The Fathers of the Church, one work at a time
about: The Fathers are the Church's first teachers after the apostles: the bishops, martyrs and monks who received the faith, defended it and handed it on. Vincent of Lérins, whose island gives this press its name, held that what they taught together, everywhere and always, is the faith itself.
Lérins Fathers prints their works one at a time, from Clement and Ignatius to John of Damascus, each in its own edition with an introduction, notes and a glossary.

collections.name: Lérins Histories
collections.tagline: Philip Schaff's History of the Christian Church
about: Philip Schaff's History of the Christian Church, in eight volumes from the apostles to the Reformation, is the standard English narrative behind the primary sources of this press. Schaff, a Swiss-born Reformed historian in America, wrote it as a Protestant who loved the Fathers and read the Church whole.
Lérins Histories prints it volume by volume, in Schaff's own order.

collections.name: Lérins Antiquities
collections.tagline: The Second Temple, the world of the New Testament
about: The Judaism our Lord and His apostles lived in, heard in its own voice. Josephus is the outside witness to Christ, to John the Baptist, to James the brother of the Lord, and to the fall of Jerusalem he watched with his own eyes. Philo of Alexandria carries the Logos vocabulary and the allegorical reading the Fathers inherited.

The Book of Enoch, quoted in the Epistle of Jude, opens with Jubilees and the Testaments the apocalyptic world the Gospels speak into. Lérins Antiquities prints them in three parts: Josephus, Philo, and the apocalyptic books.

collections.name: Lérins Empire
collections.tagline: The Roman Empire, the world of the early Church
about: The historians of the empire the Church was born into and outlived: Tacitus and Suetonius, Dio, Ammianus, and Zosimus, the last pagan to blame the Christians for Rome's fall.

Then Gibbon entire, in J. B. Bury's edition, whose notes correct the text with a century of scholarship, and Bury's own history of the later empire. Lérins Empire prints them in two parts, the imperial historians and the modern.

parts.name: Bury, and Gibbon in Bury’s edition

collections.name: Lérins Classics
about: The classical inheritance of Christendom: the poets and historians of Greece and Rome, the philosophers the Fathers argued with and learned from, the last voices of the old religion, and the older faith of the peoples who became Christendom, from the Vedas to the Eddas. The Church did not convert an empty world, but this one.

Justin Martyr, a philosopher before he was a Christian, taught that the Word had sown seeds of truth in every people, and Augustine told the Church to take back whatever the pagans had said truly, as Israel carried the gold of Egypt out with it. Lérins Classics prints those books in five parts, from Homer to Boethius.

The old religion and the new faith

collections.name: Lérins Reformers
collections.tagline: The Reformation heard in its own voice
about: The Reformation heard in its own voice: Luther in his chief works, Calvin's Institutes, John Jewel's Apology of the Church of England, and Richard Hooker's Laws of Ecclesiastical Polity.
Each of them claimed the old paths, the Scriptures and the Fathers, against the Church of his day. Lérins Reformers prints them in their own words, so the reader may judge.

collections.name: Lérins Chesterton
collections.tagline: G. K. Chesterton's case for the faith, made to the common reader
about: G. K. Chesterton made the case for the creed to the common reader in three books: Heretics (1905), Orthodoxy (1908) and The Everlasting Man (1925).
Lérins Chesterton prints them for the reader they were written for.
